title: Burak Çetin
text: It's good to see robotics finally getting the recognition it deserves these days. The venture capital market says so, the steady flow of talent says so, and of course so does the progress in AI, which promises that the physical world can be automated, despite being so unpredictable and messy for machines. That's exactly why I wanted to shine a light on the people building in the robotics space. They're a bit like Renaissance men. Their skills go way beyond writing code. They have to bridge software with the real world, and despite how it might sound, that's an incredibly hard challenge. Atoms are harder to control than bits. Here are just some of the fields a roboticist must be aware of: → Software engineering & robotics frameworks: Fluency in Python/C++ and tools like ROS 2 and simulators. Modern robots are software-defined, so code quality is critical. → AI & ML for perception and control + data: Computer vision, sensor fusion, and deep/reinforcement learning. Knowing when to use classical vs. learned methods is key. → Systems integration & mechatronics: Understanding how sensors, actuators, electronics, and embedded systems fit together. Debugging across the hardware/software boundary sets strong engineers apart. → Control theory & motion planning: From PID and MPC to trajectory optimization and path planning. This is what makes robots move reliably in the real world. → Collaboration & safety-aware design: Communicating across disciplines and designing for reliability and safety standards. Deployment realities and failure modes matter as much as features. Hats off to all these great people working in robotics space, and focusing on really hard problems :) Image credits: Jia-Bin Huang ~~ ♻️ Join the weekly robotics newsletter, and never miss any news → ziegler.substack.com

text: IL MULTIBEAM NON BASTA Puoi avere un ottimo multibeam. E fare comunque un pessimo rilievo. Ne parliamo nella seconda puntata di RILEVARE SOTT’ACQUA | Dal suono al dato. text: How can a spacecraft perform a collision avoidance manoeuvre while maintaining its operational pointing requirements? In the new journal article “Analytical Collision Avoidance with Pointing Constraints”, Eduardo Polli , Juan Luis Gonzalo Gómez and Camilla Colombo present an analytical framework for the autonomous design of fuel-optimal impulsive collision avoidance manoeuvres subject to pointing constraints. The research was developed within the COMPASS PoliMi at Politecnico di Milano and received funding from the European Union’s Horizon Europe programme through the #GREENSPECIES project. 🔗 https://lnkd.in/ektiZz-R #SpaceSafety #CollisionAvoidance #SpaceDebris #PolimiSustainability #PolimiResearch

title: OceanWings
text: ⚓️ What does it take to bring wind propulsion onto a working bulk carrier? In the latest issue of Dry Bulk magazine, OceanWings’ Romain GRANDSART explores the retrofit of the Maria Topic and what the project can tell us about the wider potential for wind-assisted propulsion in the dry bulk sector. “Working With The Wind” looks at the practical realities of integrating a wingsail on an operational vessel, while preserving cargo operations, and at the importance of building real-world performance data to support future projects. It’s great to see wind propulsion being discussed in the pages of a leading technical voice for the dry bulk industry where fuel efficiency, emissions reduction and operational practicality increasingly need to go hand in hand. 📖 Read the article from page 40 of the latest issue of Dry Bulk (free registration required): https://lnkd.in/ehrvTkQP #WindPropulsion #DryBulk #Shipping
author: OceanWings

title: Open Ocean Robotics
text: At DEFSEC Atlantic, a hot topic is how we can defend the longest coastline in the world without adding more crew or larger vessels. As a robotics guy and systems designer, my natural response is to build a team of systems that each do one thing extremely well, and get them talking to each other. Today at #DEFSECAtlantic , I signed an MOU with Sam Macdonald , building a partnership between ENVGO and Open Ocean Robotics to do exactly that. Open Ocean's solar-powered DataXplorer USVs have logged more than 13,000 hours at sea. Persistent surveillance is the first piece of the puzzle. ENVGO's XV2 sprints to a mission area at up to 25 knots to deliver rapid response and real time reconnaissance across our sovereign waters. Together, that's more eyes on the water, with the speed to respond. Sovereign Canadian technology, built in Canada for our Canadian Coast Guard/Garde côtière canadienne and Canadian Armed Forces | Forces armées canadiennes . 🇨🇦 Thanks to Julie Angus , Sam MacDonald and the whole Open Ocean Robotics team. It's just the beginning. #ENVGO #MaritimeSecurity #USV #MarineAutonomy #defence #DEFSECAtlantic2026
